newsitem.title: USA: U.S. optimistic on future of Korea talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. optimistic on future of Korea talks.

text.p: U.S. officials remained optimistic on Friday about prospects for launching four-nation Korean peace talks but ruled out negotiating North Korea's demand for a withdrawal of American forces from South Korea.

"We've deployed our troops there for a very good reason. It's a very dangerous place. And we see no reason now to speculate on what would change in an area this dangerous," State Department spokesman James Rubin told reporters.
He called negotiating the withdrawal of 37,000 U.S. troops from South Korea "a non-starter."
Another senior administration official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told Reuters: "We are not going to negotiate with the North about our troop presence."
But Rubin did not foreclose a possible change in the American deployment under certain future conditions, like improved security on the Korean peninsula.
"I'm not going to speculate on what would lead us to change our deployment," he told a news briefing.

Three days of preparatory talks in New York this week failed to reach final agreement on procedures for substantive negotiations planned for Geneva and involving the United States, China, South Korea and North Korea.
The peace negotiations, proposed by Washington and Seoul last year, are aimed at replacing the fraying armistice from the 1950-53 Korean War with a more durable peace agreement.
While U.S. officials hoped for agreement on procedures this week, they said they were not suprised that Pyongyang's negotiating team was unable to make a final decision.

"North Korea has a certain style of negotiating. Over and over we have seen that there is a first go-around. Then they recalibrate and carry proposals back to Pyongyang, work within their system and then what they come back to us with is different," one official said.
This week's outcome "strikes everybody (U.S., Chinese and South Korean negotiators) as pretty predictable at this stage," said the official, who spoke anonymously.

Rubin said the U.S. team was pleased because they "got a lot of work done", including agreement on Geneva as the site for the formal negotiations and a time -- six weeks after a follow-up preparatory meeting set for Sept. 15 in New York.

The four parties also agreed that senior officials at the level of assistant secretary of state would head each country's negotiating team, that the United States would chair the first meeting and subsequent negotiating sessions would be rotated among the other three nations.
What the U.S. side called a "significant" disagreement was over whether the agenda should be specific or general.

Rubin said "the difference is an important one, because we do not want the negotiations to be bogged down with issues that are non-starters like U.S. withdrawal of troops from the Korean peninsula, or a U.S.-DPRK (North Korea) separate agreement."
North Korean negotiators demanded that the withdrawal of U.S. forces from South Korea and a proposed separate peace between Pyongyang and Washington be on the agenda.
U.S. officials said there was a "laundry list of complaints on all sides" that had built up over the 45 years since the armistice was signed.
The United States, South Korea and China agreed that these should not be debated line-by-line in New York but as part of the substantive negotiations in Geneva, officials said.

Asked if he thought the American forces issue would dominate the Geneva negotiations, provided they happen, a U.S. official said "at bottom, we're talking about reassuring all parties on security ... U.S. troops are not the problem on the Korean peninsula."
